frictions: Both available secondary runtimes degraded with reason=tree-mutation, runtime_exit=3, on the same prompt (digest f351472844ff5fea). codex applied the M1 mutation from the brief's mutation table (removing the absolutisation in file_uri_of_path); opencode deleted 9 lines from lsp_extractor.ml, i.e. one of the new diagnostics. So the mandatory cross-runtime pass is structurally unavailable here, not merely flaky: 2 of 2 runtimes reproduce the experiments described in the prompt instead of reporting observations about them.

Hypothesis worth testing before blaming the runtimes: the prompt embeds the impl brief, which contains a mutation table naming exact code edits (M1..M5). A runtime given write access and a list of mutations may reasonably read it as work to perform. The wrapper's tree-integrity snapshot caught it both times, which is the safeguard working.
methods: restored the tree after each degraded run and verified `git diff HEAD --stat` was empty before continuing, rather than trusting the wrapper's cleanup
inspected what each runtime mutated before discarding its output — the mutation itself is information even when the findings are void
suggestion: xruntime-review should either strip mutation-table-like sections from the prompt it forwards, or state in the forwarded prompt that the runtime has read-only intent and any edit voids the run. Right now the prompt hands a runtime an explicit list of code edits and then fails it for making them.

frictions: Four review rounds, every one finding something real. The recurring class was never the code and never the intent — it was a claim about coverage that the coverage did not support. Round 2's was the sharpest: a scripted edit whose anchor no longer matched, and Python silently does nothing when the pattern is absent, so the brief asserted a fix with byte-identical code behind it.

Round 3's fix (report_once) shipped with zero coverage because the existing stub refuses EVERY request, so documentSymbol fails, no functions are extracted, and the site under test is never reached. A stub that is too aggressive is indistinguishable from a stub that works, and the test still passes.

QA's first pass NO-GO'd on a missing library, having run in the default opam switch. It escalated an environment diagnosis into a verdict on the branch, and explicitly disbelieved a measurement I had taken correctly.

Reported a copyright gate as passing when the script does not exist in this repo — the exit code came from tail inside a pipe. Third instance this session of reading an exit code from the wrong process.
methods: Mutation as the unit of proof: 21 mutants, 20 killed, each run through the command the report cites. The one survivor is documented as a survivor.
Assert the anchor of every scripted edit. One assertion fired and caught a no-op edit.
Counts, not containments, whenever the property IS the number. contains cannot tell 3 from 126.
Bound a delta by what CANNOT have changed: 3292 edges outside the touched file were raw-byte-identical, which bounds the golden's +2 without trusting any normalisation.
Verify at production scale, not only on the fixture: 91 diagnostics across 91 files on 2603 functions, where the fixture only ever showed 3 on 3.
suggestion: roster-qa should hard-verify its toolchain before running any gate, and be forbidden from returning NO-GO on a missing-dependency error without first printing proof that the environment was right. A missing library is an environment diagnosis, not a verdict on a branch — and an agent that converts one into the other produces exactly the false red that trains people to bypass gates.

frictions: Committed the completed fix directly onto local `main` instead of a feature branch — forgot to `git checkout -b` before implementing. Recovered by branching main at that commit and `git reset --hard` on main back to origin's tip, but that hard reset ALSO discarded unrelated pre-existing uncommitted work that had been sitting in the working tree all session (a doc-comment line-offset fix, +13/-1 in runner.ml, untracked test file, main.ml registration). A real near-miss: that work was gone from the working tree with no git object ever created for the exact reset moment, and was only recoverable because it had been git-stash-pushed-and-popped earlier in the session, leaving a dangling stash commit findable via `git fsck --unreachable`. Recovered in full and verified byte-identical to the pre-reset diff, but this should never have been possible to get into.

the general lesson: `git reset --hard` discards uncommitted changes to TRACKED files with no recovery path unless they were staged, stashed, or committed at some point — untracked files survive, tracked-but-modified files do not. Before any hard reset, always check git status first and stash -u anything uncommitted, even when the reset target is believed to only affect commits you made yourself.
methods: created the feature branch pointing at the accidental main-commit SHA before resetting main, so the actual fix work was never at risk — only the incidental pre-existing WIP was

recovered the pre-existing WIP via git fsck --unreachable --dangling to find the dropped stash's commit object by its custom message, then git stash apply <sha> to restore it, then diffed the result against what had been read earlier in the session to confirm byte-identical recovery
suggestion: before running `git reset --hard` for any reason, always run `git status --porcelain` first and stash -u anything present, even when confident the reset is scoped to a commit boundary and not working-tree state — the two are not the same thing and conflating them is exactly how this happened
